screens.title: Diagnosing and Resolving Replication Problems
screens.narratorSegment: In this module you will learn how to diagnose the most common causes of MySQL replication failure and how to act safely to recover a broken slave. We start by learning how to read the slave status output, understand the two replication threads, and find the exact error reported by the S Q L thread. Then we'll walk through common errors you will encounter in practice — duplicate primary key inserts and missing rows — and show the diagnostic signs and step-by-step resolutions that administrators use. You'll also see how network problems and long transactions cause input and output errors and lag, and when to use multi-threaded replication or a full resynchronization. Throughout, I will emphasize safety: always stop replication before making changes, and avoid blindly skipping events unless you accept the data divergence risks. By the end of this lesson you will be able to interpret Last_IO_Error and Last_SQL_Error, use sql_slave_skip_counter responsibly, and perform a controlled CHANGE MASTER TO when a re-point or full restore is required. Think about the last time you investigated a server log — what value would precise status fields add to diagnosing that incident?

Diagnosing and Resolving Replication Problems

Understand the root causes of replication breakage, interpret slave status, and perform safe recovery actions to keep data consistent.

Master → Slave flow
I/O reads logs • SQL applies events
In this lesson
Read slave status, identify thread errors, and use safe recovery steps.
Coming up
Resolve 1062 and 1032 errors, diagnose IO issues, and decide when to resync.
Why it matters
Timely fixes prevent divergence and protect application correctness.
Quick topics: SHOW SLAVE STATUS, sql_slave_skip_counter, CHANGE MASTER TO
Visual Summary
Master logs
Binary logs on master store events in sequence.
Slave I/O
I/O thread reads master's binary log and writes relay logs.
Slave SQL
SQL thread applies relay log events to the slave database.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical troubleshooting skills you will use as a DBA. First, you will be able to identify common causes of replication failures and explain why the slave stopped applying events. Second, you will interpret SHOW SLAVE STATUS output to find the failed thread, read error codes, and locate the binary log positions needed for recovery. Third, you will recognize specific replication errors such as duplicate-key and missing-row conditions, and apply the documented countermeasures safely so you do not create hidden divergence. Fourth, you will perform controlled recovery actions, including stopping replication, skipping events when acceptable, using CHANGE MASTER TO to reposition the slave, or deciding when a full resync is required. Each competency links to a verified milestone: ensure Slave_SQL_Running is Yes after resolution, or confirm a resync completed successfully. These are practical, testable skills for production environments and will prepare you to respond quickly while protecting data integrity.

screens.title: What does a replication failure mean?
screens.narratorSegment: A replication failure is a state where a slave server stops applying events from the master's binary log, and over time this leads to data divergence between master and slave. The two threads on a slave are critical: the input and output thread reads the master binary log into relay logs, and the S Q L thread applies those relay events to the local data. If either thread fails, the slave stops moving forward. Common causes include an S Q L error when applying an event, network disconnection preventing input and output from reading logs, or pre-existing data differences such as a manually inserted conflicting row. Why this matters: applications expecting identical reads from master and slave will see inconsistent results, and automated failover can break if replicas are not in sync. A common misconception is to treat Seconds_Behind_Master as a definitive error indicator — non-zero lag can be acceptable during long master transactions. Always inspect Last_IO_Error and Last_SQL_Error for actual failures. A practical initial check is to run SHOW SLAVE STATUS and confirm both Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are Yes. If not, the status fields guide the next recovery steps.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › What does a replication failure mean?
Definition

A replication failure happens when the slave stops applying events from the master's binary log. The slave's I/O thread or SQL thread reports an error and halts progress.

Common causes
  • SQL errors applying an event (duplicate key, missing row)
  • Network connectivity loss for the I/O thread
  • Manual, unsynchronized changes on the slave causing divergence
Misconception
Seconds_Behind_Master is not always an error; it estimates lag but does not identify the failing thread or an error code.
Key Takeaway

Use SHOW SLAVE STATUS to locate which thread failed and read Last_SQL_Error or Last_IO_Error before taking action.

Analogy
Think of the master as a publisher and the slave as a subscriber. If the subscriber's network disconnects, it stops receiving updates. If the subscriber cannot apply an update because it conflicts with local data, it stops applying further updates.
Quick checklist
  • Run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G
  • Confirm Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running
  • Read Last_IO_Error and Last_SQL_Error for specifics
Example
SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G
-- look for: Slave_IO_Running, Slave_SQL_Running, Last_SQL_Error, Exec_Master_Log_Pos

screens.title: Reading SHOW SLAVE STATUS
screens.narratorSegment: SHOW SLAVE STATUS is the primary diagnostic command when replication stalls. Key fields provide a complete snapshot of the slave's replication threads and positions. Start by confirming Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are both Yes. If Slave_IO_Running is No, the input and output thread cannot connect or read the master's binary logs. If Slave_SQL_Running is No, the S Q L thread failed applying an event; the reason will normally be in Last_SQL_Error and Last_SQL_Errno. Use Master_Log_File and Read_Master_Log_Pos to know how much the input and output thread has read, and Relay_Log_File with Relay_Log_Pos to find what the S Q L thread has processed locally. Exec_Master_Log_Pos is the position in the master's binary log that the S Q L thread has executed up to — it helps quantify how far behind the slave is in terms of executed events. Seconds_Behind_Master gives a time-based estimate of lag but can be misleading during long transactions. When you see an error code, record Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos; these values are essential if you later need to reposition the slave with CHANGE MASTER TO or to request a specific binlog extract from the master. Always log the Last_SQL_Error text and errno for accurate troubleshooting.

keyIdea.title: Diagnostic fields
keyIdea.text: Slave_IO_Running, Slave_SQL_Running, Last_SQL_Error, Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos are the most actionable fields in SHOW SLAVE STATUS.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Reading SHOW SLAVE STATUS
SHOW SLAVE STATUS walkthrough
SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G
-- Example fields to note:
Slave_IO_Running: Yes
Slave_SQL_Running: No
Last_SQL_Error: Error_code: 1062 - Duplicate entry '2' for key 'products.PRIMARY'
Master_Log_File: mysql-bin.000123
Exec_Master_Log_Pos: 12345
Seconds_Behind_Master: 42
  • Slave_IO_Running: whether I/O thread is connected and reading.
  • Slave_SQL_Running: whether SQL thread is applying events.
  • Last_SQL_Error / errno: concrete reason for SQL thread failure.
How to use positions
Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos identify the binary log and position to which the SQL thread applied events. These are required when re-pointing or when comparing master's binlog position to the slave's progress.
Example use
If Last_SQL_Error shows Error 1062, record the Exec_Master_Log_Pos and the relay file so you can skip or resync from a known position.
Key Takeaway

Treat SHOW SLAVE STATUS as your incident start: capture fields, copy error text, and decide the next safe action.

screens.title: Error 1062 — Duplicate entry on slave
screens.narratorSegment: Error 1062 occurs when the slave's S Q L thread tries to insert a row that already exists on the slave, producing a duplicate primary key conflict. This happens when the slave's data diverged from the master — for example, a manual insert on the slave that the master later also inserted. The immediate safe sequence to attempt is: STOP SLAVE; SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter = 1; START SLAVE; then run SHOW SLAVE STATUS to validate Slave_SQL_Running is Yes. This sequence skips the single offending relay event so the S Q L thread can continue. However, skipping is only safe when you understand the consequence: the skipped event will not be applied, creating a permanent mismatch for that row. A misconception is thinking skipping repairs the data; it only bypasses the failing statement. If the skipped change was critical, perform a full resync by restoring a fresh backup from the master and reconfiguring replication with CHANGE MASTER TO. Always log the error details, positions, and backups taken before skipping. Error 1062 — Duplicate entry on slave means stop slave; set global sql_slave_skip_counter=1; start slave; — use only when you accept the single-event divergence risk; otherwise resync.. In practical terms, cause, safe resolution steps, and risks of skipping events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Error 1062 — Duplicate entry
Cause

Slave tried to insert a row that already exists locally. Often due to manual changes on the slave or prior divergence.

Resolution steps (common)
STOP SLAVE;
SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter = 1;
START SLAVE;
SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G
Risk
Skipping permanently ignores the master event, leaving the slave's row inconsistent with the master for that key.
Example scenario
Slave has INSERT id=2 by manual maintenance. Later master INSERT id=2 occurs and is replicated. Slave SQL thread errors with Error_code: 1062.
Alternative
If data integrity is critical, avoid skipping and instead resync the slave from a fresh master backup, then CHANGE MASTER TO the correct file and position.
Key Takeaway

Use sql_slave_skip_counter for one-off, low-risk events. When in doubt, prefer a full resync to maintain integrity.

screens.title: Error 1032 — Can't find record to update or delete
screens.narratorSegment: Error 1032 indicates the slave tried to UPDATE or DELETE a row that does not exist locally, even though the master had that row when it executed the statement. This points to data divergence: a prior missing insert on the slave, a manual deletion, or an interrupted replication sequence. The immediate recovery pattern mirrors the duplicate-key flow: STOP SLAVE; SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter = 1; START SLAVE; followed by SHOW SLAVE STATUS to verify the S Q L thread resumed. But skipping risks hiding the fact that the slave is now missing the master's change, creating logical differences. Before skipping, investigate whether the missing row matters to application correctness. If it does, a full resync is safer: restore a consistent copy from the master and reconfigure replication positions. A frequent misconception is assuming that repeated skips fix everything — skipping multiple related events can compound divergence and lead to data loss. Always record the failed statement and positions before taking an action. Error 1032 — Can't find record to update or delete means skip only when acceptable; otherwise restore and resync. skipping removes the master's change from the slave and can create logical gaps.. In practical terms, why it happens and how to resolve it safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Error 1032 — Can't find record
Cause and implications

Slave tried to modify a row that does not exist locally. The master had the row at execution time. This indicates earlier divergence or missing transactions on the slave.

Resolution (immediate)
STOP SLAVE;
SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter = 1;
START SLAVE;
SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G
Investigate before skipping
Capture the failed DELETE/UPDATE statement and check if the missing row is required by your application. If it is, avoid skipping and perform a resync.
When to resync
When the missing row affects correctness, restore a fresh dataset from the master and use CHANGE MASTER TO to set the correct file and position before restarting replication.
Key Takeaway

Error 1032 is a clear indicator of prior divergence. Skipping is a workaround, not a substitution for restoring correct data when correctness matters.

screens.title: Diagnosing I/O thread and network issues
screens.narratorSegment: Network interruptions and input and output thread failures are common operational causes for replication breakage. When Slave_IO_Running is No, inspect Last_IO_Error; messages like "Lost connection to MySQL server during query" or "Error connecting to master" indicate a connectivity or configuration issue. Diagnosis steps include verifying the master is running, checking network reachability with ping or a simple TCP connection test to the MySQL port, and confirming no firewall rules block the connection. Also check master's resource limits such as max_connections which might reject the slave. If the root cause is transient, you can restart just the input and output thread with STOP SLAVE IO_THREAD; START SLAVE IO_THREAD; and then verify the thread reconnects. If the network issue required a configuration change, update firewall rules or master settings and then restart the input and output thread. A common oversight is restarting the entire MySQL service before capturing error messages; always capture Last_IO_Error first. Finally, after recovery, validate replication progress by checking Read_Master_Log_Pos and Exec_Master_Log_Pos to confirm the slave is catching up. Diagnosing I/O thread and network issues means check last_io_error for connectivity messages, verify network and firewall, then restart the i/o thread or correct configuration and revalidate progress.. In practical terms, how to interpret last_io_error and recover connectivity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Diagnosing I/O thread and network issues
Typical Last_IO_Error messages
  • "Lost connection to MySQL server during query"
  • "Error connecting to master 'master_host:3306' (errno: 110 'Connection timed out')"
Diagnosis checklist
  1. Ensure master MySQL process is running.
  2. From slave, ping master and test TCP to port 3306.
  3. Check firewall and master max_connections or resource limits.
Resolution actions
If transient, try restarting I/O thread only:
STOP SLAVE IO_THREAD;
START SLAVE IO_THREAD;
SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G
When to escalate
If the slave repeatedly fails to connect, fix network/firewall or increase master's connection limits. Persisting failures may require coordinated maintenance windows.
Key Takeaway

Capture Last_IO_Error and act on the network or resource cause. Restarting the IO thread can recover from transient glitches.

screens.title: Replication lag and parallel workers
screens.narratorSegment: Seconds_Behind_Master is an estimate of how far the slave is lagging in time. It is useful for spotting performance issues but is not a definitive error indicator. High values often occur because the S Q L thread is slow to apply events, particularly when a single long-running transaction on the master creates a backlog of work for the slave. When both threads are running and Last_SQL_Error is empty, consider performance actions rather than skipping events. One practical configuration in MySQL 8.0 is multi-threaded replication: set slave_parallel_workers in the slave configuration to enable concurrent apply workers. This allows independent transactions to be applied in parallel and can dramatically reduce lag for workloads with many independent transactions. However, parallelism has trade-offs: transactions that depend on order must still be applied in sequence if they conflict. A common trap is enabling too many workers without measuring the workload, which can increase locking or out-of-order application issues. Monitor Exec_Master_Log_Pos while changing parameters and validate correctness after enabling parallel workers. Replication lag and parallel workers means use slave_parallel_workers to apply events concurrently when lag is due to apply throughput, but measure and validate correctness after enabling parallelism.. In practical terms, when seconds_behind_master matters and how to reduce lag. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Seconds_Behind_Master is an estimate of how far the slave is lagging in time. It is useful for spotting performance issues but is not a definitive error indicator. High values often occur because the S Q L thread is slow to apply events, particularly when a single long-running transaction on the master creates a backlog of work for the slave. When both threads are running and Last_SQL_Error is empty, consider performance actions rather than skipping events. One practical configuration in MySQL 8.0 is multi-threaded replication: set slave_parallel_workers in the slave configuration to enable concurrent apply workers. This allows independent transactions to be applied in parallel and can dramatically reduce lag for workloads with many independent transactions. However, parallelism has trade-offs: transactions that depend on order must still be applied in sequence if they conflict. A common trap is enabling too many workers without measuring the workload, which can increase locking or out-of-order application issues. Monitor Exec_Master_Log_Pos while changing parameters and validate correctness after enabling parallel workers. Replication lag and parallel workers means use slave_parallel_workers to apply events concurrently when lag is due to apply throughput, but measure and validate correctness after enabling parallelism.. In practical terms, when seconds_behind_master matters and how to reduce lag. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use slave_parallel_workers to apply events concurrently when lag is due to apply throughput, but measure and validate correctness after enabling parallelism.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Replication lag and parallel workers
Interpreting Seconds_Behind_Master

It measures time lag as an estimate. High values alone do not indicate corruption; they point to throughput or long transactions on the master.

Common cause
A very large transaction on the master or many independent transactions queued in the relay log for the SQL thread to apply.
Using multi-threaded replication

Set slave_parallel_workers in my.cnf to a positive value to allow concurrent apply. For example, set slave_parallel_workers = 4 to run four worker threads.

Caveat
Parallel apply helps independent transactions but can complicate ordering for conflicting statements. Test carefully before deploying to production.
Key Takeaway

When lag is due to apply throughput, increase parallel workers incrementally and validate that application-level correctness is preserved.

screens.title: Using sql_slave_skip_counter safely
screens.narratorSegment: sql_slave_skip_counter is a convenient but risky tool: it instructs the S Q L thread to skip a fixed number of relay events, often used to bypass a single problematic statement. A conservative workflow begins with STOP SLAVE to ensure no concurrent application occurs. Capture SHOW SLAVE STATUS fields and copy Last_SQL_Error text and Exec_Master_Log_Pos so you can audit what you skipped. Then increment the skip counter by one with SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter = 1 and START SLAVE. Immediately re-run SHOW SLAVE STATUS to confirm Slave_SQL_Running returned to Yes and to ensure no new errors appeared. If subsequent errors relate to the same logical operation, do not keep skipping blindly; consider restoring a fresh dataset. A common mistake is skipping events without documenting them or verifying application correctness afterward — this creates silent divergence. For critical systems where data integrity is mandatory, avoid skipping entirely and prefer a full resync from the master backup. Remember: always stop the slave before changing the skip counter to avoid race conditions. Using sql_slave_skip_counter safely means stop slave; record status and error; set global sql_slave_skip_counter=1; start slave; verify status — document skipped events and prefer resync when integrity matters.. In practical terms, a conservative workflow and when to avoid skipping. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Using sql_slave_skip_counter safely
Conservative procedure
  1. STOP SLAVE;
  2. Record SHOW SLAVE STATUS fields and Last_SQL_Error text.
  3. SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter = 1;
  4. START SLAVE;
  5. SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G and validate Slave_SQL_Running is Yes.
When not to skip
If the skipped event is critical for application correctness or if many related events will be skipped, avoid skipping and resync from master backup instead.
Documentation tip
Record the exact Last_SQL_Error, Exec_Master_Log_Pos, and the relay file name before and after skipping to preserve an audit trail.
Key Takeaway

Skipping is a targeted workaround. Use it sparingly and always with full documentation and verification steps.

screens.title: Using CHANGE MASTER TO to re-point or recover
screens.narratorSegment: CHANGE MASTER TO is the command you use when you need to reconfigure the slave's master connection or set a new binary log file and position after a restore. Typical use cases include switching to a promoted master, or after restoring data on the slave and needing to resume replication from a known position. Always STOP SLAVE before running CHANGE MASTER TO. Provide the master host, credentials, and the MASTER_LOG_FILE and MASTER_LOG_POS that correspond to the desired start point. After the change, START SLAVE and confirm the slave applies events from the specified position. A concrete example is when you've restored a snapshot taken at binlog file mysql-bin.000123 position 12345; you would use CHANGE MASTER TO MASTER_LOG_FILE='mysql-bin.000123', MASTER_LOG_POS=12345 and then START SLAVE. Safety note: make sure the position corresponds to a point where the restored data matches the master's state; otherwise you risk immediate S Q L errors or silent divergence. Record previous positions before changing so you can undo or audit the operation. Using CHANGE MASTER TO to re-point or recover means use stop slave; change master to with explicit master_log_file and master_log_pos; start slave; then verify slave_sql_running is yes and positions match expectations.. In practical terms, when and how to set a new master log file and position. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use STOP SLAVE; CHANGE MASTER TO with explicit MASTER_LOG_FILE and MASTER_LOG_POS; START SLAVE; then verify Slave_SQL_Running is Yes and positions match expectations.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › CHANGE MASTER TO
When to use
  • After restoring the slave from a backup to a known binlog position.
  • When switching replication to a new master host or promoted node.
Procedure
STOP SLAVE;
CHANGE MASTER TO
  MASTER_HOST='new_master_ip',
  MASTER_USER='repl_user',
  MASTER_PASSWORD='password',
  MASTER_PORT=3306,
  MASTER_LOG_FILE='mysql-bin.000123',
  MASTER_LOG_POS=12345;
START SLAVE;
SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G
Practical advice
Ensure the MASTER_LOG_FILE and MASTER_LOG_POS correspond exactly to the state of the restored dataset. Otherwise the SQL thread may immediately fail with errors stemming from mismatch.
Key Takeaway

CHANGE MASTER TO repositions the slave. Use it after a controlled restore or during a planned master change, and verify the slave applies events correctly.

screens.title: Deciding: skip events or full resync?
screens.narratorSegment: When you encounter a replication error, you must decide whether to skip the offending event or perform a full resynchronization. The decision depends on the error type, the importance of the data, and whether other related events will be affected. If the error is a single harmless statement and the application can tolerate missing that change, skipping may be acceptable after recording positions and logs. If the Last_SQL_Error indicates a structural mismatch or many dependent events will be skipped, choose a full resync. A full resync entails restoring a fresh backup from the master and then using CHANGE MASTER TO to point the slave to a binlog position that corresponds with the backup. The architecture view is simple: skipping is quick and targeted but adds a divergence risk; resync is authoritative and safe but costs time and resources. Always capture the status before acting, inform stakeholders if production data may be affected, and prefer resync for critical datasets. The final rule: when uncertain, err on the side of data integrity. Deciding: skip events or full resync? means skip for single, low-impact events only. resync when integrity is required or when multiple related events are involved.. In practical terms, a decision flow for choosing the appropriate recovery strategy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Deciding: skip events or full resync?
Quick decision flow
  1. Capture SHOW SLAVE STATUS and error text.
  2. Assess impact: single statement vs many dependent changes.
  3. If low impact and isolated, consider skipping with documentation.
  4. If high impact or uncertain, perform full resync from master backup.
Stakeholder step
Notify application owners when a skip or resync could change observed data to avoid surprise behavior in production.
Architecture view
Skipping keeps the slave running quickly but erodes a single source of truth. Resync reestablishes authoritative state but requires time and a maintenance window.
Key Takeaway

Balance speed versus correctness. When in doubt, prefer a full resync to protect data integrity.

screens.title: Simulate and resolve a replication error
screens.narratorSegment: This guided activity walks through a simple lab: create a table on the master, verify replication on the slave, introduce a manual conflicting row on the slave, then cause the master to insert a conflicting row to trigger Error 1062. Start by ensuring both Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are Yes and note Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos. On the master, create a table and insert a row. Confirm the slave has the row. Next, on the slave insert a conflicting row manually so the same primary key exists with different content. Then insert a row with the same key on the master; the slave's S Q L thread will error reporting Error_code: 1062. At that point stop the slave, run SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter=1, then start the slave and re-run SHOW SLAVE STATUS. Observe that Slave_SQL_Running returns to Yes and that the master's insert was skipped on the slave, demonstrating data divergence. This reinforces the operational mechanics and the consequences of skipping a replicated event. After the exercise, practice the alternative: resync the slave from a backup and reconfigure replication to see the full recovery path.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Simulate and resolve a replication error
Lab timeline
Step 1 - Prepare
Ensure replication is running and note Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos via SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G.
Step 2 - Create table and insert on master
-- On Master:
USE test_db;
CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100));
INSERT INTO products (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Laptop');
Step 3 - Diverge the slave
-- On Slave:
USE test_db;
INSERT INTO products (id, name) VALUES (2, 'Mouse'); -- manual insert
Step 4 - Trigger error
-- On Master:
INSERT INTO products (id, name) VALUES (2, 'Keyboard'); -- replicated to slave -> Error 1062
Step 5 - Resolve by skipping
-- On Slave:
STOP SLAVE;
SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter = 1;
START SLAVE;
SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G
Key Takeaway

This lab shows the immediate fix and the data divergence that results. Use it to practice documentation and to compare the skip vs resync options.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, replication failure is when the slave stops applying events; focus on the two threads — input and output and S Q L — to find the source. Second, SHOW SLAVE STATUS is your primary diagnostic tool; record Slave_IO_Running, Slave_SQL_Running, Last_SQL_Error, Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos when investigating. Third, the two most common S Q L errors you will see are Error 1062 for duplicate entries and Error 1032 for missing rows; both often reflect prior divergence and each has a documented recovery pattern. Fourth, sql_slave_skip_counter lets you skip events but can permanently diverge data; use it only when acceptable. Finally, CHANGE MASTER TO repositions a slave after a controlled restore and is part of the authoritative resync workflow. Keep these concepts as quick mental checks during incident response: diagnose, record, decide, act, and verify.

fullNarratorScript:
In this module you will learn how to diagnose the most common causes of MySQL replication failure and how to act safely to recover a broken slave. We start by learning how to read the slave status output, understand the two replication threads, and find the exact error reported by the S Q L thread. Then we'll walk through common errors you will encounter in practice — duplicate primary key inserts and missing rows — and show the diagnostic signs and step-by-step resolutions that administrators use. You'll also see how network problems and long transactions cause input and output errors and lag, and when to use multi-threaded replication or a full resynchronization. Throughout, I will emphasize safety: always stop replication before making changes, and avoid blindly skipping events unless you accept the data divergence risks. By the end of this lesson you will be able to interpret Last_IO_Error and Last_SQL_Error, use sql_slave_skip_counter responsibly, and perform a controlled CHANGE MASTER TO when a re-point or full restore is required. Think about the last time you investigated a server log — what value would precise status fields add to diagnosing that incident?

These objectives map to practical troubleshooting skills you will use as a DBA. First, you will be able to identify common causes of replication failures and explain why the slave stopped applying events. Second, you will interpret SHOW SLAVE STATUS output to find the failed thread, read error codes, and locate the binary log positions needed for recovery. Third, you will recognize specific replication errors such as duplicate-key and missing-row conditions, and apply the documented countermeasures safely so you do not create hidden divergence. Fourth, you will perform controlled recovery actions, including stopping replication, skipping events when acceptable, using CHANGE MASTER TO to reposition the slave, or deciding when a full resync is required. Each competency links to a verified milestone: ensure Slave_SQL_Running is Yes after resolution, or confirm a resync completed successfully. These are practical, testable skills for production environments and will prepare you to respond quickly while protecting data integrity.

In addition to understanding the theory, you will practice concrete steps that are common in production incidents. You will run SHOW SLAVE STATUS and interpret fields to find whether the input and output or S Q L thread is the source of failure. You will read Last_SQL_Error and Last_SQL_Errno to get an exact replication error code. You will execute the safe sequence: STOP SLAVE, apply a corrective action such as skipping a single relay event or re-pointing the master, then START SLAVE and recheck status. You will also recognize when network faults require checking port reachability and firewall rules, and when lag is due to long transactions rather than an error. Finally, you will know the conditions that demand a full resync from backup instead of a skip. Each objective reinforces reducing risk while restoring replication quickly. Practice these tasks in a sandbox before applying them on critical production servers.

A replication failure is a state where a slave server stops applying events from the master's binary log, and over time this leads to data divergence between master and slave. The two threads on a slave are critical: the input and output thread reads the master binary log into relay logs, and the S Q L thread applies those relay events to the local data. If either thread fails, the slave stops moving forward. Common causes include an S Q L error when applying an event, network disconnection preventing input and output from reading logs, or pre-existing data differences such as a manually inserted conflicting row. Why this matters: applications expecting identical reads from master and slave will see inconsistent results, and automated failover can break if replicas are not in sync. A common misconception is to treat Seconds_Behind_Master as a definitive error indicator — non-zero lag can be acceptable during long master transactions. Always inspect Last_IO_Error and Last_SQL_Error for actual failures. A practical initial check is to run SHOW SLAVE STATUS and confirm both Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are Yes. If not, the status fields guide the next recovery steps.

SHOW SLAVE STATUS is the primary diagnostic command when replication stalls. Key fields provide a complete snapshot of the slave's replication threads and positions. Start by confirming Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are both Yes. If Slave_IO_Running is No, the input and output thread cannot connect or read the master's binary logs. If Slave_SQL_Running is No, the S Q L thread failed applying an event; the reason will normally be in Last_SQL_Error and Last_SQL_Errno. Use Master_Log_File and Read_Master_Log_Pos to know how much the input and output thread has read, and Relay_Log_File with Relay_Log_Pos to find what the S Q L thread has processed locally. Exec_Master_Log_Pos is the position in the master's binary log that the S Q L thread has executed up to — it helps quantify how far behind the slave is in terms of executed events. Seconds_Behind_Master gives a time-based estimate of lag but can be misleading during long transactions. When you see an error code, record Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos; these values are essential if you later need to reposition the slave with CHANGE MASTER TO or to request a specific binlog extract from the master. Always log the Last_SQL_Error text and errno for accurate troubleshooting.

Error 1062 occurs when the slave's S Q L thread tries to insert a row that already exists on the slave, producing a duplicate primary key conflict. This happens when the slave's data diverged from the master — for example, a manual insert on the slave that the master later also inserted. The immediate safe sequence to attempt is: STOP SLAVE; SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter = 1; START SLAVE; then run SHOW SLAVE STATUS to validate Slave_SQL_Running is Yes. This sequence skips the single offending relay event so the S Q L thread can continue. However, skipping is only safe when you understand the consequence: the skipped event will not be applied, creating a permanent mismatch for that row. A misconception is thinking skipping repairs the data; it only bypasses the failing statement. If the skipped change was critical, perform a full resync by restoring a fresh backup from the master and reconfiguring replication with CHANGE MASTER TO. Always log the error details, positions, and backups taken before skipping. Error 1062 — Duplicate entry on slave means stop slave; set global sql_slave_skip_counter=1; start slave; — use only when you accept the single-event divergence risk; otherwise resync.. In practical terms, cause, safe resolution steps, and risks of skipping events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Error 1032 indicates the slave tried to UPDATE or DELETE a row that does not exist locally, even though the master had that row when it executed the statement. This points to data divergence: a prior missing insert on the slave, a manual deletion, or an interrupted replication sequence. The immediate recovery pattern mirrors the duplicate-key flow: STOP SLAVE; SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter = 1; START SLAVE; followed by SHOW SLAVE STATUS to verify the S Q L thread resumed. But skipping risks hiding the fact that the slave is now missing the master's change, creating logical differences. Before skipping, investigate whether the missing row matters to application correctness. If it does, a full resync is safer: restore a consistent copy from the master and reconfigure replication positions. A frequent misconception is assuming that repeated skips fix everything — skipping multiple related events can compound divergence and lead to data loss. Always record the failed statement and positions before taking an action. Error 1032 — Can't find record to update or delete means skip only when acceptable; otherwise restore and resync. skipping removes the master's change from the slave and can create logical gaps.. In practical terms, why it happens and how to resolve it safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Network interruptions and input and output thread failures are common operational causes for replication breakage. When Slave_IO_Running is No, inspect Last_IO_Error; messages like "Lost connection to MySQL server during query" or "Error connecting to master" indicate a connectivity or configuration issue. Diagnosis steps include verifying the master is running, checking network reachability with ping or a simple TCP connection test to the MySQL port, and confirming no firewall rules block the connection. Also check master's resource limits such as max_connections which might reject the slave. If the root cause is transient, you can restart just the input and output thread with STOP SLAVE IO_THREAD; START SLAVE IO_THREAD; and then verify the thread reconnects. If the network issue required a configuration change, update firewall rules or master settings and then restart the input and output thread. A common oversight is restarting the entire MySQL service before capturing error messages; always capture Last_IO_Error first. Finally, after recovery, validate replication progress by checking Read_Master_Log_Pos and Exec_Master_Log_Pos to confirm the slave is catching up. Seconds_Behind_Master is an estimate of how far the slave is lagging in time. It is useful for spotting performance issues but is not a definitive error indicator. High values often occur because the S Q L thread is slow to apply events, particularly when a single long-running transaction on the master creates a backlog of work for the slave. When both threads are running and Last_SQL_Error is empty, consider performance actions rather than skipping events. One practical configuration in MySQL 8.0 is multi-threaded replication: set slave_parallel_workers in the slave configuration to enable concurrent apply workers. This allows independent transactions to be applied in parallel and can dramatically reduce lag for workloads with many independent transactions. However, parallelism has trade-offs: transactions that depend on order must still be applied in sequence if they conflict. A common trap is enabling too many workers without measuring the workload, which can increase locking or out-of-order application issues. Monitor Exec_Master_Log_Pos while changing parameters and validate correctness after enabling parallel workers. sql_slave_skip_counter is a convenient but risky tool: it instructs the S Q L thread to skip a fixed number of relay events, often used to bypass a single problematic statement. A conservative workflow begins with STOP SLAVE to ensure no concurrent application occurs. Capture SHOW SLAVE STATUS fields and copy Last_SQL_Error text and Exec_Master_Log_Pos so you can audit what you skipped. Then increment the skip counter by one with SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter = 1 and START SLAVE. Immediately re-run SHOW SLAVE STATUS to confirm Slave_SQL_Running returned to Yes and to ensure no new errors appeared. If subsequent errors relate to the same logical operation, do not keep skipping blindly; consider restoring a fresh dataset. A common mistake is skipping events without documenting them or verifying application correctness afterward — this creates silent divergence. For critical systems where data integrity is mandatory, avoid skipping entirely and prefer a full resync from the master backup. Remember: always stop the slave before changing the skip counter to avoid race conditions. Using sql_slave_skip_counter safely means stop slave; record status and error; set global sql_slave_skip_counter=1; start slave; verify status — document skipped events and prefer resync when integrity matters.. CHANGE MASTER TO is the command you use when you need to reconfigure the slave's master connection or set a new binary log file and position after a restore. Typical use cases include switching to a promoted master, or after restoring data on the slave and needing to resume replication from a known position. Always STOP SLAVE before running CHANGE MASTER TO. Provide the master host, credentials, and the MASTER_LOG_FILE and MASTER_LOG_POS that correspond to the desired start point. After the change, START SLAVE and confirm the slave applies events from the specified position. A concrete example is when you've restored a snapshot taken at binlog file mysql-bin.000123 position 12345; you would use CHANGE MASTER TO MASTER_LOG_FILE='mysql-bin.000123', MASTER_LOG_POS=12345 and then START SLAVE. Safety note: make sure the position corresponds to a point where the restored data matches the master's state; otherwise you risk immediate S Q L errors or silent divergence. Record previous positions before changing so you can undo or audit the operation. When you encounter a replication error, you must decide whether to skip the offending event or perform a full resynchronization. The decision depends on the error type, the importance of the data, and whether other related events will be affected. If the error is a single harmless statement and the application can tolerate missing that change, skipping may be acceptable after recording positions and logs. If the Last_SQL_Error indicates a structural mismatch or many dependent events will be skipped, choose a full resync. A full resync entails restoring a fresh backup from the master and then using CHANGE MASTER TO to point the slave to a binlog position that corresponds with the backup. The architecture view is simple: skipping is quick and targeted but adds a divergence risk; resync is authoritative and safe but costs time and resources. Always capture the status before acting, inform stakeholders if production data may be affected, and prefer resync for critical datasets. The final rule: when uncertain, err on the side of data integrity. Deciding: skip events or full resync? means skip for single, low-impact events only. resync when integrity is required or when multiple related events are involved.. This guided activity walks through a simple lab: create a table on the master, verify replication on the slave, introduce a manual conflicting row on the slave, then cause the master to insert a conflicting row to trigger Error 1062. Start by ensuring both Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are Yes and note Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos. On the master, create a table and insert a row. Confirm the slave has the row. Next, on the slave insert a conflicting row manually so the same primary key exists with different content. Then insert a row with the same key on the master; the slave's S Q L thread will error reporting Error_code: 1062. At that point stop the slave, run SET GLOBAL sql_slave_skip_counter=1, then start the slave and re-run SHOW SLAVE STATUS. Observe that Slave_SQL_Running returns to Yes and that the master's insert was skipped on the slave, demonstrating data divergence. This reinforces the operational mechanics and the consequences of skipping a replicated event. After the exercise, practice the alternative: resync the slave from a backup and reconfigure replication to see the full recovery path.

Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, replication failure is when the slave stops applying events; focus on the two threads — input and output and S Q L — to find the source. Second, SHOW SLAVE STATUS is your primary diagnostic tool; record Slave_IO_Running, Slave_SQL_Running, Last_SQL_Error, Master_Log_File and Exec_Master_Log_Pos when investigating. Third, the two most common S Q L errors you will see are Error 1062 for duplicate entries and Error 1032 for missing rows; both often reflect prior divergence and each has a documented recovery pattern. Fourth, sql_slave_skip_counter lets you skip events but can permanently diverge data; use it only when acceptable. Finally, CHANGE MASTER TO repositions a slave after a controlled restore and is part of the authoritative resync workflow. Keep these concepts as quick mental checks during incident response: diagnose, record, decide, act, and verify.

Keep three compact reminders for rapid incident response. First, always STOP SLAVE before making state changes and capture the error text and binlog positions for auditing. Second, use sql_slave_skip_counter only for one-off, low-risk errors and document the skipped events to preserve traceability. Third, when data correctness matters or when multiple events will be affected, perform a full resynchronization from an authoritative master backup and then use CHANGE MASTER TO to re-establish replication from a verified position. These rules reduce the risk of silent divergence and ensure you can explain and recover from operational decisions made during an incident.
